summary: Overwatering and poor drainage can cause yellowing and dropping leaves, wilting, soft stem bases and soggy soil, and can lead to root decay.

distinguishing_questions.question: Does the soil stay wet for days after watering?
Does water drain out of the bottom of the pot?

next_actions: Let the soil dry as much as possible between waterings
Make sure water can drain from the container
inspect_next: Pull the plant out and check whether the roots are white and firm or dark and soft
caveats: Wilting can also come from underwatering or too much light, so check the roots and soil.

summary: Wilting is usually caused by underwatering or excessive light. Brown leaf tips or margins can result from excessively dry soil.

distinguishing_questions.question: Is the soil dry well below the surface?
Does the plant perk up after watering?

next_actions: Re-check the plant after watering
inspect_next: Check whether the soil pulls away from the pot or is dry deep down
caveats: Root decay from overwatering also causes wilting, so inspect the roots before assuming the plant is too dry.

summary: Root rot is often seen as wilting or discoloration above ground. Off-color roots (brownish to blackish), especially at the tips, indicate root rot; healthy roots are white. It is often associated with poor drainage and overwatering.

distinguishing_questions.question: Are the roots dark and soft when you slide the plant out of its pot?
Has the soil been staying wet or draining poorly?

next_actions: Improve drainage and watering frequency
Remove rotted portions and repot the healthy sections in fresh, well-drained mix (UMD)
inspect_next: Slide the plant out of the pot and look at the roots
caveats: Severely damaged plants may be best discarded (UMD).

summary: Brown leaf tips or margins are usually caused by overfertilization, salt buildup, or excessively dry or wet soil. Fertilizer salts can also build up on containers.

distinguishing_questions.question: Has the plant been fertilized often, or is there a white crust on the soil or pot?
Does tap water leave deposits on the pot?

next_actions: Flush the soil with clear water to leach excess salts
Scrub the edges of the pot (Illinois)
inspect_next: Look for crust on the soil surface and pot rim
caveats: Other causes of brown tips include too much sun or heat, low humidity and drafts.

summary: Yellow-green older leaves can be due to insufficient fertilizer, especially nitrogen. Weak growth or light green to yellow leaves may also come from root rot, too little or too much light, or sap-sucking pests.

distinguishing_questions.question: Are the older, lower leaves yellowing first?
Has the plant gone a long time without fertilizer or repotting?

next_actions: Consider a water-soluble fertilizer after fixing watering (Illinois)
Repot into a larger container if root bound (Illinois)
inspect_next: Check whether the plant is root bound
caveats: Yellowing on older leaves can also come from poor root health, low light or sap-sucking pests.

cause: micronutrient deficiency or soil pH imbalance
summary: Yellow-green newer leaves can be caused by overwatering, soil pH imbalance or micronutrient deficiency.

distinguishing_questions.question: Is the yellowing on the newest leaves rather than the oldest?
Has the soil been staying wet?

next_actions: Rule out overwatering first
inspect_next: Compare new leaves with older leaves
caveats: The source does not give specific tests for pH or micronutrients.

summary: Leggy growth with long stems or petioles is usually caused by inadequate light. Lack of flowers can indicate inadequate light, and yellowing and leaf drop can also be caused by inadequate light.

distinguishing_questions.question: Is the plant far from a window or in a dim room?
Is new growth long, thin and stretched toward light?

next_actions: Move the plant closer to a light source or add artificial light
inspect_next: Note how far the plant is from the nearest window
caveats: Excess fertilizer can also cause spindly growth (UMD).

summary: Excess light can bleach or whiten leaves and cause spots or blotches, especially after a recent move of the plant.

distinguishing_questions.question: Was the plant recently moved into brighter light or outdoors?
Is the damage on the side facing the window?

next_actions: Move the plant to a less sunny spot
Acclimate plants slowly to higher light (UMD)
inspect_next: Check which leaves get direct sun
caveats: Fungal and bacterial spots can look similar.

summary: Chilling injury below 50°F can cause leaf spots and blackening of leaves or shoots. Symptoms may continue for up to a week after exposure.

distinguishing_questions.question: Was the plant recently near a cold window, door or draft?
Did temperatures drop below about 50°F?

next_actions: Protect plants from temperatures below 50°F
Re-check in about a week, since symptoms can keep appearing
inspect_next: Check where the plant sits at night

summary: Brown leaf tips or margins may result from low relative humidity, too much sun or heat through a window, or a drafty setting, in addition to watering and fertilizer problems.

distinguishing_questions.question: Is the plant near a heater, vent or drafty door?
Is the air in the room very dry?

next_actions: Rule out watering and salt buildup first
caveats: Erratic watering and drafts are also listed by Illinois as causes of brown edges.

summary: Many plants go through an adjustment period anytime they are moved, even short distances. Yellowing or leaf drop that continues more than a few weeks suggests another problem.

distinguishing_questions.question: Was the plant recently moved, repotted or brought home?
Has it been more than a few weeks since the move?

next_actions: Give the plant a few weeks in favorable conditions
If it continues, change its location and watering schedule

summary: Poor root health from pot-bound growth, compacted soil or poor drainage is listed as a cause of yellowing, leaf drop and sudden wilting.

distinguishing_questions.question: Are roots circling the inside of the pot or coming out of the drainage holes?
Has the soil become hard or compacted?

next_actions: Repot into fresh soil (Illinois)
inspect_next: Slide the plant out of the pot to look at the roots

summary: Spider mites are tiny and usually on leaf undersides. Feeding causes light-colored specks (stippling), later bronzing and drying, and silk webbing may appear near growing points. Severe infestations cause leaves to dry and fall.

distinguishing_questions.question: Is there fine webbing on or under the leaves?
Do you see tiny pale specks on the leaves?

next_actions: Wash leaf surfaces with water frequently
Reduce dust
Dispose of infested plant parts
Isolate the plant to prevent spread
inspect_next: Look at leaf undersides, with a hand lens if you have one
caveats: Low humidity and dusty conditions favor mites. Thrips can cause similar stippling.

summary: Mealybugs are small, oval, whitish insects covered in cottony, powdery or waxy material, often along leaf veins or where leaf stalks join stems. Symptoms include stunted growth, yellowing and wilting; they excrete honeydew and attract ants.

distinguishing_questions.question: Is there white cottony material in leaf joints or along veins?
Are the leaves sticky?

next_actions: Wash or scrape them off
Dab individual mealybugs with 70% or weaker rubbing alcohol on a cotton swab, testing a small area first
Dispose of infested plant parts
Isolate the plant
inspect_next: Check crevices, leaf bases and flower clusters, and the roots
caveats: Rubbing alcohol is flammable. Heavy infestations may be best handled by discarding the plant.

summary: Aphids are small insects on new growth or leaf undersides. They excrete sticky honeydew that can attract ants and encourage sooty mold, leave white cast skins, and can cause leaves to curl and distort.

distinguishing_questions.question: Do you see small soft-bodied insects clustered on new growth?
Are there white cast skins or sticky residue?

next_actions: Wash them off with a spray of water
Remove, bag and dispose of infested plant parts
Isolate the plant
inspect_next: Check new growth and leaf undersides

summary: Scales are small brown or grayish, mostly stationary insects with a waxy or hard covering. They suck sap and excrete honeydew, giving leaves a sticky surface and later stunting growth and discoloring leaves. On ferns they can resemble spore clusters.

distinguishing_questions.question: Are there raised brown bumps on stems or leaves that can be scraped off?
Are the leaves sticky?

next_actions: Scrape them off
Wash off crawling young stages with water
Dispose of heavily infested parts or the plant (Illinois)
inspect_next: Check crevices, leaf bases and leaflet folds

summary: Adult whiteflies are small white to yellowish winged insects that fly up when the plant is disturbed. Young stages stay on leaf undersides, suck sap and excrete honeydew, causing leaves to yellow and drop.

distinguishing_questions.question: Do tiny white insects fly up when you touch the plant?
Are there small immobile insects on leaf undersides?

next_actions: Wash eggs and crawling young off with water
Dispose of infested plant parts
Isolate the plant
Yellow sticky traps may reduce adults
inspect_next: Check leaf undersides
caveats: Large infestations may be best handled by discarding the plant.

summary: Thrips are small slender insects usually on leaf undersides and in tight crevices. They cause scarring, sometimes distorted growth, stippling similar to mites, shiny black dots of excrement, and yellowing and dropping leaves; heavy infestations can leave silvery-gray areas.

distinguishing_questions.question: Do you see shiny black dots on the leaves?
Is the stippling accompanied by silvery-gray patches rather than webbing?

next_actions: Wash them off with water
Dispose of infested plant parts
inspect_next: Check leaf undersides and flowers
caveats: Thrips damage looks similar to spider mite stippling.

summary: Adult fungus gnats are small, dark, mosquito-like flies seen near potted plants or lights. Larvae in moist soil feed on roots; heavy infestations can cause sudden wilting, poor growth and foliage loss. Overwatering and poor drainage favor them.

distinguishing_questions.question: Do small dark flies rise from the soil when you disturb it?
Does the soil stay moist for long periods?

next_actions: Let the soil dry as much as possible between waterings
Eliminate standing water
Remove old plant debris
Yellow sticky traps may trap adults
inspect_next: Look at the soil surface and near windows or lights for adult flies

summary: Broad and cyclamen mites are nearly invisible and are recognized by injury on new growth: thickened, brittle foliage with stunted, downward-cupped margins. Cyclamen mites are mainly a pest of flowering plants and can cause few flowers.

distinguishing_questions.question: Is the damage on the newest growth?
Are leaf edges cupped downward and brittle?

next_actions: Frequently wash leaf surfaces with water
Dispose of infested plant parts
Cyclamen-mite infested plants are best discarded (UMD)
inspect_next: Compare new growth with older leaves
caveats: Chemical injury can cause similar symptoms, so mite damage is easily misidentified.

summary: Powdery mildew shows as white to gray growth on leaves, flowers and stems; the growth is the fungus itself on the tissue surface. It usually will not kill the plant but can cause defoliation.

distinguishing_questions.question: Does the white coating sit on the surface and look like powder?
Is the plant in a humid spot with poor air flow?

next_actions: Improve air circulation
Pick off infected leaves
Reduce humidity by watering early in the day, moving to brighter light and away from cold drafts
inspect_next: Check leaves, flowers and stems

summary: Gray mold mainly infects spent flowers and older foliage, appearing as grayish or tan areas with dusty gray spores. It needs high humidity for several hours and is usually not serious unless it stays cool and wet.

distinguishing_questions.question: Is the fuzzy growth on old, faded flowers or older lower leaves?
Has foliage stayed wet or the air been humid?

next_actions: Remove spent or infected flowers and foliage
Increase air circulation and reduce humidity
Avoid splashing water on foliage and flowers
Water early in the day
inspect_next: Check old flowers and lower leaves

summary: Fungal leaf spots are tan to reddish-brown to black, roughly circular spots that may merge into large lesions. They spread by splashing water and need hours of leaf wetness.

distinguishing_questions.question: Are the spots roughly round with a defined edge?
Has water been splashing onto the leaves?

next_actions: Avoid splashing water on foliage
Water early in the day
Remove and discard infected leaves promptly
Improve air circulation
inspect_next: Check both sides of spotted leaves
caveats: UC IPM says foliar leaf spots are usually not a problem indoors; sunburn, chilling, overwatering and chemical injury cause similar spots.

summary: Localized bacterial diseases appear as oily, greasy or water-soaked spots, often visible from the leaf underside, that may turn tan, brown or black with a yellow border and enlarge until the whole leaf is affected.

distinguishing_questions.question: Do the spots look oily or water-soaked, especially from underneath?
Do the spots have a yellow border?

next_actions: Lower humidity and keep plant surfaces dry
Promptly remove infected parts
Wash hands with soap and disinfect pruning tools in 70% alcohol after removing infected parts
inspect_next: Look at leaf undersides and nearby stems

cause: systemic bacterial stem rot or wilt
summary: Systemic bacterial diseases can cause wilting, general yellowing, and soft, mushy stem rots or cankers that may smell unpleasant. Control options are very limited and discarding the plant is often the best approach.

distinguishing_questions.question: Is the stem soft or mushy, possibly with a bad smell?

next_actions: Avoid splashing water, contaminated hands and pruning tools
Water sparsely and fertilize lightly
Consider discarding the plant
inspect_next: Check the stem base for soft, mushy tissue
caveats: Overwatering can also cause soft stem bases.

summary: Stem cankers appear as discolored areas on the stem and can be associated with wilting.

distinguishing_questions.question: Is there a discolored patch on the stem?

next_actions: Prune out affected areas
inspect_next: Check stems for discolored areas

summary: Viruses cause foliage to appear mottled green and yellow, and plants may be stunted or distorted. There is no effective treatment.

distinguishing_questions.question: Is the leaf color patchy green and yellow rather than evenly yellow?
Is the plant also stunted or twisted?

next_actions: Discard infected plants
Isolate the plant first
inspect_next: Compare several leaves for the mottled pattern
caveats: Aphids and mites can also cause stunted, distorted growth, so rule out pests.

summary: Leaves that are eaten or chewed may be caused by pests on plants that spent the summer outside, such as caterpillars, leaf-feeding beetles, weevils, grasshoppers, crickets, slugs and earwigs.

distinguishing_questions.question: Has the plant been outdoors recently?
Are there ragged holes or chewed edges, possibly with droppings or slime?

next_actions: Handpick pests
Repot plants before moving them inside
inspect_next: Check the plant and soil for the chewing pest

summary: Brown or scorched leaf tips and spots or blemishes can result from pesticide or mechanical injury, and chemical spray injury is listed as a cause of leaf spots.

distinguishing_questions.question: Was the plant recently sprayed or bumped?

inspect_next: Think back to recent sprays or handling
caveats: Heavy mite feeding can leave plants vulnerable to injury from insecticidal sprays (UMD).
